title: Getting to Yes: Negotiating Agreement Without Giving In
publication: Houghton Mifflin, Boston (1st ed.); 2nd ed. 1991 and 3rd ed. 2011 with Bruce Patton (Penguin)
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors (Roger Fisher, William Ury), 1981 first edition with Houghton Mifflin, later editions (1991, 2011) adding Bruce Patton, the four principles of principled negotiation and the origin of the term BATNA matched on en.wikipedia.org and an EBSCO Research Starters entry (ebsco.com). No publisher page was found in search results, so the URL is a reference page rather than the publisher’s.

summary: The founding practitioner text of “principled negotiation”, written by members of the Harvard Negotiation Project. It argues for separating the people from the problem, focusing on interests rather than positions, inventing options for mutual gain and insisting on objective criteria. It introduced the term BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) as the standard against which any proposed agreement should be measured.
arguments: Positions are what parties say they want; interests are why they want it. Agreements built on interests are easier to find and more durable.
Your BATNA, not a fixed “bottom line”, is the proper benchmark for judging a proposed deal; developing it starts with listing what you could do if no agreement is reached.
Objective criteria (market data, precedent, professional standards) let parties settle distributive questions without a contest of wills.
design: Prescriptive book drawing on the authors’ practice and teaching; not an empirical study.
strengths: Clear, durable vocabulary (interests, options, criteria, BATNA) that most later research and teaching adopted; usable immediately.
limitations: Practitioner prescription, not tested evidence. Critics argue it underplays the distributive side of bargaining and the role of power; its examples are illustrative rather than systematic.
contested: Its advice to focus on interests and joint gains is broadly consistent with later laboratory work on integrative bargaining (e.g. R-thompson-1990-social), but the book itself presents no data, and its treatment of value claiming is thinner than analytic treatments such as R-lax-1986-manager and R-raiffa-1982-art.
generalizability: High as a preparation vocabulary across industries and in sport; the claims about what works best should be treated as heuristics to test.
relevance: Gives you the core vocabulary for this week (interests, BATNA, objective criteria) and the language most counterparts, agents and lawyers will use with you.

title: The Art and Science of Negotiation
publication: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, Cambridge, MA
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, year (1982), publisher (Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, Cambridge, MA), x + 373 pages and ISBN 0674048121 matched in the CiNii catalogue (ci.nii.ac.jp) and the Weber State University library catalogue; the book’s structure (two-party single-issue bargaining, two-party multi-issue bargaining, many-party negotiations; Panama Canal and Camp David cases) matched in catalogue and bookseller descriptions. A 1985 paperback exists.

summary: A decision analyst’s treatment of negotiation that moves from two parties bargaining over one issue, to two parties with many issues, to negotiations among many parties. It combines analytic models with cases such as the Panama Canal and Camp David negotiations, and is widely described as a bridge between popular negotiation advice and formal game theory.
arguments: Negotiation can be analyzed systematically: each party’s alternatives and reservation values define whether a zone of agreement exists.
Multi-issue bargaining differs in kind from single-issue haggling because parties can trade across issues they value differently.
Negotiations with many parties introduce coalitions and dynamics that two-party models do not capture.
design: Analytic monograph combining formal models with historical cases.
strengths: Rigor; separates what a single negotiator can calculate from what depends on the other side; a foundation for later analytic approaches to negotiation.
limitations: Written before most of the behavioral research on negotiator bias; some formal material is demanding; historical cases are illustrations, not tests.
generalizability: The analytic structure (alternatives, reservation values, multi-issue trades, coalitions) transfers to any deal; the behavioral assumptions should be checked against later research.
relevance: The analytic backbone for lessons 1 and 2: it teaches you to treat a negotiation as a structured decision rather than a contest of personalities.

title: The Manager as Negotiator: Bargaining for Cooperation and Competitive Gain
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, publisher (Free Press) and year (c1986) matched in the CiNii catalogue (ci.nii.ac.jp) and on the publisher’s site (simonandschuster.co.uk, Free Press is a Simon & Schuster imprint); Chapter 2, “The Negotiator’s Dilemma: Creating and Claiming Value”, pp. 29–45, matched in University at Buffalo course reading guides (acsu.buffalo.edu).

summary: Treats managers as negotiators inside and outside their organizations and builds “negotiation analysis” from case work, decision analysis, game theory and psychology. Its best-known idea is the negotiator’s dilemma: the moves that create value (sharing information, joint problem solving) leave you exposed to the moves that claim it (withholding information, committing to favorable terms), and the two activities cannot be separated.
arguments: Creating value and claiming value are inextricably linked; advice that addresses only one of them is incomplete.
Sharing information about priorities makes joint gains possible but can be exploited by a counterpart who claims aggressively.
Managers negotiate constantly with colleagues and constituencies, not only with outside parties.
design: Analytic book built on extensive case analysis plus decision analysis, game theory and psychology.
strengths: Holds the cooperative and competitive sides of bargaining in one frame; written for managers; widely adopted in graduate teaching.
limitations: Conceptual rather than empirical; the dilemma is a framework, not a measured effect.
generalizability: High: the creating–claiming tension appears in vendor deals, internal budget talks, employment negotiations and partnerships.
relevance: Required reading (Chapter 2). It names the tension you will feel in the Negotiation Chamber: every question you answer about your priorities helps the deal and helps the other side.

title: Negotiation and Conflict Management (15.667, Spring 2001)
publication: MIT OpenCourseWare, MIT Sloan School of Management
license: CC BY-NC-SA (MIT OpenCourseWare). Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Course number, title, term (Spring 2001), instructor (Prof. Mary Rowe), graduate level, Sloan School of Management, syllabus, readings, assignments and study-materials pages, and the Creative Commons BY-NC-SA license matched on ocw.mit.edu; a syllabus record by Mary Rowe also appears on dspace.mit.edu.

summary: An openly licensed graduate course on negotiation theory, strategies and styles in an employment context. Its eleven sessions run from an introduction through distributive bargaining, cultural differences, dispute prevention, mediation and dealing with difficult people. The site provides the syllabus, calendar, reading lists and handouts on conflict styles and bargaining tactics.
arguments: Negotiation skill in organizations includes conflict management with colleagues, not only deal making with outsiders.
Different conflict styles (competing, compromising, avoiding and others) suit different situations; knowing your default is a starting point.
Workplace conflict benefits from a range of options, from direct negotiation to mediation and formal processes.
design: University course materials (syllabus, readings list, handouts); not a study.
strengths: Free, openly licensed, written for working professionals, and unusually focused on conflict inside organizations.
limitations: Materials date from 2001–2002; some readings are commercial textbooks not reproduced on the site; handouts are teaching tools, not evidence.
generalizability: High for internal and employment negotiations; the course frames are practitioner tools rather than tested models.
relevance: Required reading. It shows how a graduate program frames negotiation as part of everyday management, which is where most of your negotiating happens.

title: First offers as anchors: The role of perspective-taking and negotiator focus
publication: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 81(4), 657–669
license: © American Psychological Association. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMID 11642352); faculty listings at london.edu and kellogg.northwestern.edu agree. Findings below are taken from the PubMed abstract.

summary: Three experiments on buyer–seller price negotiations found that whichever side made the first offer, buyer or seller, obtained the better outcome, and that first offers strongly predicted final prices. The first-offer advantage disappeared when the recipient focused on information inconsistent with the offer: the offerer’s alternatives, the offerer’s reservation price, or the recipient’s own target. The effects appeared in face-to-face and e-mail negotiations.
arguments: A first offer works as an anchor: it pulls the final settlement toward itself.
Making the first offer advantaged the offerer regardless of role (buyer or seller).
Recipients can neutralize an anchor by deliberately focusing on the other side’s alternatives or reservation price, or on their own target.
design: Three laboratory experiments with simulated price negotiations, face-to-face and by e-mail.
strengths: Experimental control; tests both the effect and practical countermeasures; consistent with the broader, well-replicated anchoring literature.
limitations: Simulated single-issue price negotiations with student participants; modest stakes; does not test what happens when an anchor is so extreme that it ends the conversation, or when the offerer lacks information.
contested: The basic anchoring effect is among the more robust findings in judgment research, but the size of first-offer advantages in high-stakes field negotiations is less well established than the lab evidence; treat the countermeasure findings as promising rather than settled.
generalizability: Moderate to high for price-like issues where the value is uncertain (fees, salaries, budgets); lower when both sides have reliable market data.
relevance: Required reading. It turns the “should I go first?” question into a reasoned choice and gives you a tested defense when the other side anchors.

title: Social perception in negotiation
publication: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 47(1), 98–123
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 47, issue 1, pages 98–123 and year matched on ideas.repec.org and on kellogg.northwestern.edu faculty research listings. The DOI was not shown in search results, so it is omitted. Findings below are taken from abstract-level descriptions and citing work.

summary: A study of how negotiators perceive the other side’s interests. It reports that most negotiators enter a negotiation expecting the other party’s interests to be completely opposed to their own, and argues that such misperceptions of the other side’s interests are a primary cause of agreements that leave joint value unclaimed. It is the standard citation for the “fixed-pie” perception.
arguments: Negotiators commonly assume the pie is fixed: whatever one side gains, the other loses.
Misjudging the other side’s priorities leads to inefficient agreements, not just tougher bargaining.
Accurate perception of the counterpart’s interests is a learnable source of joint gains.
design: Laboratory negotiation simulation with measures of negotiators’ judgments of the other party’s interests (details beyond the abstract not confirmed here).
strengths: Identifies a perceptual mechanism behind inefficient deals; foundational for later integrative-bargaining research.
limitations: Lab simulation with structured point tables; real negotiations often have genuinely opposed interests, so the fixed-pie assumption is sometimes correct.
contested: Later work notes that a fixed-pie perception is not always inaccurate; the error is assuming it without checking. The mechanism is well accepted; its magnitude in the field is less studied.
generalizability: High as a caution for multi-issue deals (contracts, partnerships, budgets); limited for genuinely single-issue, one-shot haggling.
relevance: Explains why intelligent people split the difference on every issue and leave value behind, the mistake the Negotiation Chamber is designed to expose.

title: A meta-analysis on gender differences in negotiation outcomes and their moderators
license: © American Psychological Association. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, all six authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched on the University of Münster research portal (cris-portal.uni-muenster.de); scope (51 studies, 10,888 participants, several countries) and the moderator findings matched in the APA press release (apa.org, December 2014). Published online November 2014, in the 2015 volume.

summary: A meta-analysis of 51 studies (10,888 participants, several countries) comparing the economic outcomes women and men obtain in negotiations. The difference favoring men depended heavily on context: women did better when negotiating on behalf of another person, when they had information about the bargaining range, and when they had negotiation experience. The pattern points to situational rather than fixed-trait explanations, and the authors highlight ways the difference can be lessened or reversed.
arguments: Gender differences in negotiated economic outcomes are context-dependent rather than fixed.
Advocating for someone else, experience, and information about the bargaining range were associated with smaller differences, and in some conditions with women doing better.
Reducing ambiguity about what is negotiable and what the range is can shrink gaps.
design: Meta-analysis of 51 studies reporting final economic negotiation outcomes by gender, with moderator analyses; extends an earlier meta-analysis by Stuhlmacher and colleagues.
strengths: Large pooled sample across countries; moderator analyses directly useful for organizational design.
limitations: Mostly laboratory and classroom negotiations; moderator effects are correlational across studies; gender is measured as a binary category; economic outcomes only (not relationships or subjective value).
contested: Popular claims that women “don’t negotiate” or are uniformly worse negotiators are not supported by this evidence, which shows strong situational moderation; the size of field gaps in real compensation negotiations remains debated.
generalizability: Moderate: the moderators (advocacy role, information, experience) are plausible levers in organizations, but effect sizes from lab studies should not be transferred to field settings without caution.
relevance: Teaches you to read a meta-analysis on a sensitive topic carefully, and points to design choices you control: publishing ranges, clarifying what is negotiable, and how you structure compensation conversations for your staff.

title: Cultural differences in ultimatum game experiments: Evidence from a meta-analysis
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched on cambridge.org, econpapers.repec.org and the Tinbergen Institute site (tinbergen.nl). A free working-paper version (EconWPA, January 2004, ewp-exp/0401003) appeared in search results. Findings below come from the abstract.

summary: A meta-analysis of 37 papers reporting 75 ultimatum-game results. Proposers offered on average about 40 percent of the pie. Responder behavior, not proposer behavior, varied across regions; rejection rates were lower for larger pies and larger offered shares, and responders were less willing to accept under the strategy method. With one exception, regional differences could not be explained by standard cultural classifications (Hofstede, Inglehart).
arguments: People routinely offer far more than the “rational” minimum in the ultimatum game, and responders reject offers they see as unfair.
Variation across regions shows up mainly in what responders accept.
Popular national-culture scores explain little of that variation, a caution against stereotyping by country.
design: Meta-analysis of 75 results from 37 ultimatum-game papers, regressing offers and rejections on study features and regional/cultural indicators.
strengths: Pools many experiments; tests cultural explanations explicitly rather than assuming them.
limitations: Stylized one-shot game with mostly student samples; regional coding is coarse; small stakes in many studies.
contested: Whether ultimatum-game behavior reflects stable fairness preferences or context-specific norms is debated; this meta-analysis cautions against simple national-culture explanations.
generalizability: Moderate: the core lesson (offers perceived as unfair get rejected even at a cost) travels well; specific percentages do not transfer to complex deals.
relevance: Shows why fairness is a constraint you must design for in any deal, and why “they will accept anything above their alternative” is poor executive reasoning.

title: Negotiation behavior when cultures collide: The United States and Japan
license: © American Psychological Association. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 86, issue 3, pages 371–385 and year matched in the ACNP union catalogue index (acnpsearch, University of Bologna) and a bibliographic database; the DOI was listed by one index and follows the journal’s DOI pattern. Findings below come from the abstract.

summary: Japanese and U.S. managers negotiated an integrative task with partners from their own culture and from the other culture; transcripts were coded and analyzed. U.S. negotiators shared information directly and avoided influence tactics within and across cultures; Japanese negotiators shared information indirectly and used influence with each other but adapted their behavior in intercultural negotiations. Culturally typical behaviors partly explained why intercultural pairs reached lower joint gains than intracultural pairs.
arguments: Cultures differ in how negotiators exchange information (direct questions and answers versus indirect inference from offers).
Intercultural pairs reached lower joint gains than same-culture pairs, partly because their information-exchange routines did not mesh.
Negotiators can and do adapt their behavior when they cross cultures; adaptation is part of the skill.
design: Simulation with Japanese and U.S. managers in intra- and intercultural dyads; coded transcripts analyzed with logistic and linear regression.
strengths: Managers rather than students; behavioral coding of what negotiators actually said; links behavior to joint gains.
limitations: Two countries only; one simulation; culture measured by nationality, which hides large within-country variation.
contested: National culture as an explanatory variable is debated: individual and regional variation is large, and meta-analytic evidence in other bargaining paradigms finds weak links to cultural indices (R-oosterbeek-2004-cultural).
generalizability: The mechanism (mismatched information-exchange routines lower joint gains) plausibly transfers to other cross-cultural pairs; the specific U.S.–Japan profiles do not.
relevance: Gives you an evidence-based way to think about cross-border negotiations, including those in Latin America, without relying on national stereotypes.

title: Artful paltering: The risks and rewards of using truthful statements to mislead others
publication: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 112(3), 456–473
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 112, issue 3, pages 456–473 and date (March 2017; online December 2016) matched on hks.harvard.edu and in the APA press release (apa.org, December 2016). The DOI did not appear in search results, so it is omitted. Findings come from the abstract and press release.

summary: Defines paltering as the active use of truthful statements to create a misleading impression, distinct from lying by commission (false statements) and lying by omission (passively not sharing). Across pilot studies and six experiments (over 1,750 participants), paltering in negotiation helped palterers claim value but also raised the likelihood of impasse and harmed their reputations when detected. Targets judged paltering about as unethical as lying; palterers and observers judged it more favorably.
arguments: Paltering is common and many people prefer it to outright lying.
It can claim value in the short run but increases impasse risk and reputational damage.
Targets treat paltering as the ethical equivalent of a false statement, a perception gap palterers underestimate.
design: Two pilot studies and six experiments, including negotiation tasks, with more than 1,750 participants in total.
strengths: Names and measures a tactic that ethics codes often miss; multiple studies; includes the target’s perspective.
limitations: Laboratory and online samples with modest stakes; detection is engineered by the design; legal consequences are not studied.
contested: No independent replication of the negotiation studies was confirmed in our search; treat this as a multi-study paper from one research team, consistent with but not yet established by other work.
generalizability: Moderate to high: repeated-game settings (staff, agents, vendors, partner organizations) make the reputational costs larger than in one-shot lab tasks.
relevance: Draws the line most executives blur: technically true but misleading statements. Essential for an executive whose reputation is a long-term negotiating asset.

title: Ethical and unethical bargaining tactics: An empirical study
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 17, issue 6, pages 665–682 and year matched on philarchive.org and a library discovery record; sample and findings (320 Ohio State and 736 Harvard Business School MBA students rating 18 tactics on a 1–7 scale; five factors) matched in the Ohio State University news release (news.osu.edu). The DOI was not shown in search results.

summary: Surveyed MBA students at two business schools (320 and 736 respondents) on how appropriate they considered 18 bargaining tactics. Factor analysis found five clusters of tactics that were similar across the two samples. Tough but not outright dishonest tactics, such as inflating an opening demand, were widely accepted; outright lies and bribery were widely rejected. Acceptability differed by sample, gender, age and work experience, and nationality.
arguments: Negotiators distinguish “traditional competitive bargaining” (e.g. inflated opening demands) from misrepresentation, bluffing about facts and bribery.
There is broad agreement at the extremes and real disagreement in the middle of the spectrum.
Judgments of acceptability vary with personal characteristics and context, so your counterpart’s ethics may not match yours.
design: Cross-sectional survey of two MBA samples rating the appropriateness of 18 tactics; factor analysis and group comparisons.
strengths: Large samples; replicated factor structure across two schools; gives a shared vocabulary for tactic types.
limitations: Self-reported judgments of hypothetical tactics by MBA students; acceptability is not the same as behavior; data from the 1990s.
generalizability: Moderate: useful as a map of where norms agree and disagree; actual behavior under pressure may differ from stated judgments.
relevance: Helps you write a personal policy for the grey zone of bargaining and predict where counterparts will draw their own lines.
